connection: Session 13 studied IEnumerable<ClockEntry>, itself a generic interface. This session steps back to name what T actually means, using generic types already at work throughout the real codebase -- List<ClockEntry>, Dictionary<int, Employee>, Task<ClockEntry?> -- plus one new generic method, GenericRules.Later<T>.
objectives: Identify at least three generic types already in real, everyday use across this codebase, and state what concrete type argument each is instantiated with.
Explain why IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry returns Task<ClockEntry?> specifically, not just Task -- what the type argument communicates.
Read GenericRules.Later<T>(T left, T right) and explain why it can compare 'left' and 'right' generically without knowing T is DateTime or int in advance.
Call Later<T> with both DateTime (ClockIn timestamps) and int (EmployeeId values) and confirm one method definition serves both.

visuals.title: Generic types are filled in at each use site
visuals.explanation: List<ClockEntry>, Dictionary<int, Employee>, and Task<ClockEntry?> are the same three generic type definitions (List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, Task<TResult>) each instantiated differently.

visuals.title: A generic method infers T from its arguments
visuals.explanation: GenericRules.Later(entryA.ClockIn, entryB.ClockIn) infers T as DateTime from the arguments' actual type -- no explicit Later<DateTime> is required.

visuals.title: Task<ClockEntry?> says exactly what eventually arrives
visuals.explanation: The T in Task<T> is the type of value the asynchronous operation eventually produces -- here, possibly-null ClockEntry, matching GetClockEntry's real nullable contract.

visuals.title: One method definition, many closed types
visuals.explanation: Later<DateTime> and Later<int> are two different closed generic methods generated from the one open Later<T> definition, at compile time.

preQuiz.prompt: What are List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, and Task<TResult> called before a concrete type is supplied?
options: Open generic types -- they define a shape with placeholder type parameters that must be filled in (with ClockEntry, or int and Employee, or ClockEntry?) at the point of use
preQuiz.explanation: A generic type definition like List<T> is not usable on its own -- List<ClockEntry> is the closed, concrete type actually declared and used.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry return Task<ClockEntry?> instead of plain Task?
options: Task<T> carries a result value once the asynchronous operation completes; plain Task represents an operation with no result at all -- GetClockEntry needs to eventually hand back a ClockEntry? value, so it needs the generic form
Task<T> is required for every async method regardless of return value
preQuiz.explanation: ClockIn's IClockEntryService.ClockIn method, by contrast, is synchronous void -- and Clockout returns plain Task because it produces no result value, only completion. GetClockEntry needs Task<ClockEntry?> specifically because it DOES produce a result.

preQuiz.prompt: Can GenericRules.Later<T> be called with both DateTime and int arguments, using the same method definition?
options: Yes -- as long as the argument type implements IComparable<T> (both DateTime and int do), the compiler generates a specific closed version of Later<T> for each type used
No -- a separate Later method must be written for each type
Only with int, since DateTime cannot be compared
preQuiz.explanation: This is the entire value of generics: one definition, reused across every type that satisfies its constraint -- Session 15 studies that constraint directly.

concept.title: Generic types already everywhere in this codebase
paragraphs: ClockEntryRepository._clockEntries is List<ClockEntry> -- List<T> with T filled in as ClockEntry. EmployeeDirectory's employees field is Dictionary<int, Employee> -- Dictionary<TKey,TValue> with two type arguments supplied. IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry returns Task<ClockEntry?> -- Task<TResult> with TResult filled in as the nullable ClockEntry type.
None of these are new concepts introduced by this session -- they are the same generic types Sessions 5-12 already used, named explicitly here for the first time.
concept.code:
List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries;              // List<T> with T = ClockEntry
Dictionary<int, Employee> employees;         // Dictionary<TKey,TValue> with TKey=int, TValue=Employee
Task<ClockEntry?> GetClockEntry(int employeeId, ...);  // Task<TResult> with TResult = ClockEntry?

concept.title: A generic method: one definition, many closed forms
paragraphs: GenericRules.Later<T>(T left, T right) where T : IComparable<T> works for any type T that can compare itself to another T -- DateTime and int both implement IComparable<T> in the .NET base class library.

Calling Later(entryA.ClockIn, entryB.ClockIn) lets the compiler infer T as DateTime from the argument types; calling Later(employeeA.EmployeeId, employeeB.EmployeeId) infers T as int. No explicit type argument is required at either call site.

concept.title: Why not just write two separate methods?
paragraphs: A non-generic LaterDate(DateTime, DateTime) and LaterId(int, int) would duplicate the exact same >= 0 comparison logic twice, with only the type name different.

Later<T> expresses that duplication as one piece of logic, parameterized over any comparable type -- this is the same motivation as IEnumerable<T> in Session 13: write the capability once, apply it to many concrete types.

lab.objective: Call GenericRules.Later<T> with both DateTime and int arguments from the real domain, and confirm one method definition serves both without modification.
lab.startingCondition: GenericRules.Later<T> already exists with the real where T : IComparable<T> constraint.
steps: Call Later with two ClockEntry.ClockIn values and confirm the later of the two DateTimes is returned.
Call Later with two Employee.EmployeeId values and confirm the greater int is returned.
Attempt to call Later with two Employee objects directly (not their EmployeeId), and observe the compile error -- Employee does not implement IComparable<Employee>.
Explain, in writing, why that compile error is the constraint working as intended, not a bug.
lab.expectedBehavior: Later(DateTime, DateTime) and Later(int, int) both compile and return the correct result; Later(Employee, Employee) fails to compile with a constraint-violation error.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Confirm the real generic method and its IComparable<T> constraint.
Confirm coverage across at least two different closed generic types.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

commit: session-13: teach generic types and methods
review: Every generic type cited is quoted from real, already-existing code, not invented for this session.
Later<T> is demonstrated with two genuinely different closed type arguments, not just described abstractly.
The Employee compile-error case is used to make the constraint's purpose concrete, not skipped.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can List<ClockEntry> and Dictionary<int, Employee> both exist in the same codebase using the same underlying generic collection library?
options: List<T> and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> are separate generic type definitions in .NET's base class library, each independently instantiated with whatever type arguments the codebase needs
They are the same generic type used two different ways
Dictionary is built from List internally in every case
postQuiz.explanation: List<T> and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> are distinct generic types -- the shared idea is only that both defer their element/key/value types to a type parameter, filled in at each declaration.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if GenericRules.Later<T> had no constraint at all (just Later<T>(T left, T right))?
options: left.CompareTo(right) would fail to compile -- without a constraint, the compiler only knows T could be any type, including one with no CompareTo method at all
It would work exactly the same for every type
T would default to object automatically
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly what Session 15 studies next -- without the where T : IComparable<T> constraint, the compiler cannot assume CompareTo exists on an arbitrary T.

postQuiz.prompt: Does calling Later(entryA.ClockIn, entryB.ClockIn) require writing Later<DateTime>(...) explicitly?
options: No -- the compiler infers T as DateTime from the argument types automatically; explicit type arguments are only needed when inference is ambiguous or impossible
Yes -- generic methods always require an explicit type argument
No -- but only because DateTime is a built-in type
postQuiz.explanation: Type inference from arguments is standard for generic methods in C# -- explicit type arguments (Later<DateTime>(...)) are optional here and rarely needed.

reflections: Why does writing Later<T> once, instead of LaterDate and LaterId separately, matter beyond saving a few lines of code?
What other places in this codebase might benefit from a generic helper like Later<T>, once you start looking for duplicated type-specific logic?
How does Task<ClockEntry?> communicate more to a reader than plain Task would, at the exact call site where GetClockEntry is awaited?
whatBreaks: Calling GenericRules.Later with two Employee arguments (instead of their EmployeeId or another IComparable value) fails to compile, because Employee implements no comparison logic -- this is the constraint doing its job, not a limitation to work around. Removing the where T : IComparable<T> constraint would let Later<T> compile against any T, but left.CompareTo(right) inside the method body would then fail to compile, since the compiler could no longer assume CompareTo exists.
summary: Generic types are not a new concept this session invents -- List<ClockEntry>, Dictionary<int, Employee>, and Task<ClockEntry?> were already doing real work throughout Sessions 5-12. GenericRules.Later<T> demonstrates the other half of generics: one method definition, reused unmodified across every type (DateTime, int, and any future IComparable<T>) that satisfies its constraint.
